Unit 1 — Introduction to Operations Research

 1.1 Origin of OR

 OR began in England during World War II. British (and later American) military executives needed to allocate scarce
 resources to military operations effectively.

 Teams of specialists from engineering, mathematics, statistics, economics, psychology, etc. were formed to do “research on
 (military) operations”.

 This joint research produced strategies for search operations, flight patterns, convoy survival (speed, size), radar deployment,
 etc. (Notes: Feb 1917 convoy work; 1935 radar was born.)

 After the war OR spread to industry and business and developed rapidly.

Milestones in OR

 Year Milestone

 1948 OR Club formed in England, later the Operations Research Society of U.K.

 1950 Operations Research Society of America formed

 1950s OR recognised as a subject of academic study at degree level by many universities

 1953 Operations Research Institute at Indian Statistical Institute, Calcutta

 1957 Operations Research Society of India; first major application by Prof. Mahalanobis to formulate India’s 2nd Five-Year Plan

 1957 International Federation of OR Societies (IFORS), headquarters in London



 1.2 Definitions of OR

 OR is the use of the scientific method to provide criteria for decisions regarding man–machine–money systems involving
 repetitive operations. It provides managers with a quantitative basis for decision making.


It now symbolises a scientific, interdisciplinary team approach that mathematically analyses issues such as agriculture, natural
resources, management, international trade, industrial production, quality and productivity. In short: the field of study which
gives you the ability for decision-making (analytic method). (Notes)

 Author / body Definition

 Operations Research Society of “OR is concerned with scientifically deciding how to best design and operate man–machine
 America systems, usually requiring the allocation of scarce resources.”

 D.W. Miller & M.K. Starr “OR is applied decision theory. It uses any scientific, mathematical or logical means to attempt to
 cope with the problems that confront the executive when he tries to achieve a thorough-going
 rationality in dealing with his decision problems.”

 Daellenbach & George “OR is essentially a collection of mathematical techniques and tools which, in conjunction with a
 system approach, are applied to solve practical decision problems of an economic or engineering
 nature.”

 H.M. Wagner “OR is a scientific approach to problem solving for executive management.”

Thierauf & Klekamp “OR utilises the planned approach (updated scientific method) and an interdisciplinary team in
 order to represent complex functional relationships as mathematical models for the purpose of
 providing a quantitative analysis.”

 H.A. Taha “OR is a scientific knowledge through interdisciplinary team effort for the purpose of determining
 the best utilisation of limited resources.”


Changing business environment — why OR is needed

 Competition forces organisations to be more competitive and productive, and to perform better in growth and quality.

 Financial and human-resource planning have become critical; “lots of data, business changing” (notes).

 Therefore every “operation” in a business requires “research”. Industry, planning & inventory, transport, military,
 government and information systems all use the OR approach.

 Decision making is the key managerial skill; a fruitful decision results from a rigorous, scientific approach.


 1.3 What is Operations Research? — key terms

 Term Meaning

 Operations The activities carried out in an organisation.

 Research The process of observation and testing characterised by the scientific method: situation, problem
 statement, model construction, validation, experimentation, etc.

 Model An abstract representation of reality — mathematical, physical, narrative, or a set of rules in a computer
 program.

 Optimal solution A solution to the model that optimises (maximises or minimises) some measure of merit over all feasible
 solutions.

 Team A group of individuals bringing various skills and viewpoints to a problem.

 OR techniques A collection of general mathematical models, analytical procedures and algorithms.

 Optimisation (notes) The process of finding the best possible solution while maximising efficiency and minimising cost, time or
 resources.



 1.4 Significant features of OR

 1. Decision-making tool — its main aim is to help management take better decisions.

 2. Scientific approach — uses the scientific method (observe → hypothesise → model → test → implement).

 3. Inter-disciplinary team approach — experts from many fields work together.

 4. Use of digital computers — real OR models are large; software (Excel Solver, TORA) solves them.

 5. Objectives — looks for the best (optimal) result for the whole system/organisation, considering all its objectives (system
 orientation).


 1.5 Concept of optimising a performance measure

Every OR problem has a measure of performance (effectiveness) E — profit, cost, time, distance, utilisation — that depends on
variables we can control and variables we cannot:



Unit 1 · Introduction to OR Made by Jay Naik Page 4 of 124

E = f (Xc, Xuc) subject to constraints gi(Xc, Xuc) ≤ / = / ≥ bi

where Xc = controllable (decision) variables, Xuc = uncontrollable variables (parameters). Optimising means choosing Xc so that E
is maximised (profit, output) or minimised (cost, time) while every constraint is respected. In an LPP the performance measure is
the objective function Z, the controllable variables are x1, x2, … and the uncontrollable variables are the coefficients (prices,
capacities). The main object of a model is to maximise the utility of the system by controlling the controllable variables.

 1.7 Deterministic vs stochastic optimisation

 Deterministic optimisation Stochastic (probabilistic) optimisation

 All parameters (costs, demands, capacities) are known exactly Some or all parameters are random variables that take values
 and fixed at predetermined values — no uncertainty. with given probabilities.

 Same input always gives the same output. Output is described by expected values, variances, probabilities.

 Examples: LPP, IPP, transportation, assignment, CPM, basic EOQ Examples: queuing models, PERT (random activity times),
 model. simulation, stochastic inventory.

 Solved by exact algorithms (simplex, Hungarian, MODI). Solved by probability theory, expected-value models or
 simulation.



 1.8 Models in OR

 A problem is expressed in terms of a model — a theoretical approximation of a real-life problem (“representation of our
 problem”).

 The model’s purpose is to analyse the behaviour of the system in order to improve its performance.

 Factors significant to the solution are variables: controllable or uncontrollable. An OR model is a mathematical description of
 these variables; it shows how changes in one or more variables affect the rest of the problem.

 Mathematical models comprise controllable variables, uncontrollable variables and result variables.

 1.9 Phases (methodology) of an OR study

1. Formulate the problem — analyse the physical system; set the objective; determine constraints; identify
 controllable/uncontrollable variables, alternative courses of action and the measure of effectiveness.

2. Construct the model — establish the measure of effectiveness and constraints, then express them as functions of the system
 variables: E = f(Xi, Yj), X controllable, Y uncontrollable.

3. Acquire the input data — accurate, complete data (reports, company documents, interviews); quality of data determines
 quality of output.

4. Solve the model — find values of decision variables that optimise the objective, by analytical, numerical or simulation
 methods. Sensitivity analysis is used when data are inaccurate or assumptions doubtful.




Unit 1 · Introduction to OR Made by Jay Naik Page 6 of 124

5. Test the solution (model validation) — the model is valid if it contains all relevant objectives, constraints and decision
 variables, its functional relationships are valid, and it reliably predicts the real system (insignificant variables may be omitted).

 6. Implement the solution — translate it into workable procedures with management participation; if it is not implemented,
 the research is incomplete. The OR team prepares detailed instructions.

 7. Modify the model — if validation shows the model does not predict the real system, identify omitted or incorrect
 constraints, reconsider the formulation, update regularly.

 8. Establish controls over the solution — feedback on variables that deviate significantly; control the solution as a whole and
 the values of variables under changing conditions.

Unit 2 — Linear Programming Problem (LPP)

 2.1 Formulation of an LPP

 A Linear Programming Problem is the problem of optimising (maximising or minimising) a linear objective function of
 decision variables subject to a set of linear equality/inequality constraints and non-negativity restrictions.


Components of an LPP (notes)

1. Decision variables x1, x2, …, xn — the unknown quantities we control (units to produce, money to invest).

2. Objective function — Max or Min Z = c1x1 + … + cnxn (profit, cost, yield, reach); cj = contribution per unit.

3. Constraints — limits on resources/requirements: ai1x1 + … + ainxn (≤, =, ≥) bi.

4. Non-negativity restriction — xj ≥ 0 (decision variables cannot be negative).


Steps of formulation (notes)

1. Identify the decision variables (and define them with units).

2. Set the objective function (what is maximised/minimised).

3. Identify the constraints (one for each limited resource or requirement; “at least” → ≥, “at most / not exceed” → ≤, “exactly”
 → =).

4. Write the non-negativity restrictions.


 Example 2.1 — Formulation: investment (pension fund) Source: Handwritten notes (OR Devyani Notes), Q2

 A pension fund has Rs. 30 million to invest in treasury notes, bonds and stocks. Rules: at least Rs. 3 million in each type; at
 least half the money in treasury notes and bonds; the amount in bonds must not exceed twice the amount in treasury
 notes. Annual yields: treasury notes 7%, bonds 8%, stocks 9%. Allocate the money to maximise yield.

 Decision variables: x1 = amount (Rs. million) in treasury notes, x2 = in bonds, x3 = in stocks.


 Maximise Z = 0.07x1 + 0.08x2 + 0.09x3
 subject to
 x1 + x2 + x3 ≤ 30 (total money; = 30 if all must be invested)
 x1 ≥ 3, x2 ≥ 3, x3 ≥ 3 (at least 3 million each)
 x1 + x2 ≥ 15 (at least half of 30 in notes + bonds)
 x2 ≤ 2x1 i.e. −2x1 + x2 ≤ 0 (bonds ≤ twice notes)
 x1, x2, x3 ≥ 0


 Solution (by reasoning): stocks earn most, so put as much as possible in stocks: x1 + x2 = 15 (minimum), x3 = 15. Between
 notes and bonds, bonds earn more, so make x2 as large as allowed: x2 = 2x1 → 3x1 = 15 → x1 = 5, x2 = 10. Zmax = 0.35 + 0.80
 + 1.35 = Rs. 2.5 million.

General and matrix form of an LPP

 Optimise Z = c1x1 + c2x2 + … + cnxn
 subject to ai1x1 + ai2x2 + … + ainxn (≤, =, ≥) bi, i = 1, …, m
 xj ≥ 0, j = 1, …, n


Matrix form: Max (or Min) Z = C X subject to A X (≤, =, ≥) b, X ≥ 0, where C = (c1, …, cn) is the 1×n cost/profit row vector, X =

(x1, …, xn)T the n×1 decision vector, A = [aij] the m×n coefficient (technology) matrix and b = (b1, …, bm)T the m×1 requirement
(RHS) vector. Standard form (used by simplex): all constraints equations (add slack / subtract surplus), all bi ≥ 0, all variables ≥ 0.

Example (Example 2.4): C = (5, 2), A = [[2, 6], [6, 2]], b = (24, 24)T, so Max Z = (5 2)(x1 x2)T, [[2 6],[6 2]] X ≤ (24, 24)T.


Implicit assumptions of LPP

 Assumption Meaning

 Proportionality Contribution of each variable to Z and to each constraint is directly proportional to its value (double x →
 double profit and double resource use).

 Additivity Total = sum of individual contributions; no interaction terms (no x1x2).

 Divisibility (continuity) Variables may take fractional values (if not acceptable → Integer Programming, Unit 3).

 Certainty (deterministic) All coefficients cj, aij, bi are known constants.

 Linearity Objective and constraints are linear functions.

 2.2 Geometry of LPP — convex sets, extreme points, basic feasible solutions

Term Definition

Solution Any set of values of the decision variables.

Feasible solution Any non-negative solution that satisfies all the constraints.

Feasible region The region that represents the collection of all feasible solutions.

Optimal solution A feasible solution that gives the best (max/min) value of Z.

Hyperplane The set {X : a1x1 + … + anxn = b} — a line in 2-D, a plane in 3-D. Each constraint boundary is a
 hyperplane.

Half-plane / half-space A linear inequality in two variables is called a half-plane (a1x1 + a2x2 ≤ b); together with its boundary it
 is a closed half-plane.

Convex set A set S such that the line segment joining any two points of S lies wholly in S: if X1, X2 ∈ S then λX1 +
 (1−λ)X2 ∈ S for 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1. (Circle, triangle, polygon region: convex; a crescent or star: not convex.)

Convex polygon / polyhedron The intersection of a finite number of closed half-planes (constraints) — always a convex set. The
 feasible region of an LPP is a convex polyhedron (possibly unbounded or empty).

Extreme (corner) point / vertex A point of a convex set that does not lie on the segment joining any two other points of the set — the
 vertices of the convex polygon.

Basic solution For m equations in n variables (n > m), set (n − m) variables = 0 (non-basic) and solve for the remaining
 m (basic) variables.

Basic feasible solution (BFS) A basic solution with all basic variables ≥ 0. Every BFS corresponds to an extreme point of the feasible
 region.

Degenerate BFS A BFS in which one or more basic variables are zero.

Redundant constraint A constraint that does not change the feasible region (removing it leaves the region unchanged).

Multiple (alternate) solution Same optimal value of Z for different values of (x1, x2).

Unbounded solution Z can be increased (Max) or decreased (Min) indefinitely — typically when constraints are “≥” for a
 Max problem, e.g. Max Z = 2x1 + 4x2, x1 ≥ 50, x2 ≥ 100 (notes).



 Fundamental theorems. (1) The feasible region of an LPP is a convex set. (2) If an LPP has an optimal solution, at least one
 extreme point is optimal (this is why we only test corners). (3) Every BFS is an extreme point and vice-versa. (4) The
 maximum number of basic solutions = nCm = n! / (m!(n − m)!).

 2.3 Graphical method (two variables)

1. Step 1: Convert/consider each inequality constraint as an equation.

2. Step 2: Put one variable = 0 and find the other — this gives one point (intercept) on the line.

3. Step 3: Similarly find a second point by putting the second variable = 0.

4. Step 4: Plot the line through both points.

5. Step 5: Repeat for all constraints and identify the feasible region (satisfies all constraints and x1, x2 ≥ 0). Test the origin: if
 (0,0) satisfies the inequality, the feasible side contains the origin.

6. Step 6: Find the coordinates of each vertex (corner point) — solve the two intersecting lines simultaneously — and put them
 in the objective function; the best value is the optimum (corner-point method). Alternatively slide an iso-profit / iso-cost line
 parallel to the objective until it last touches the region.

2.4 Simplex method

The graphical method works only for 2 variables. The simplex method (G.B. Dantzig, 1947) is an iterative algebraic procedure
that moves from one basic feasible solution (corner) to an adjacent better one until no improvement is possible.

Terminology

 Term Meaning

 Slack variable (s ≥ 0) Added to a ≤ constraint to make it an equation: unused resource. Coefficient 0 in Z.

 Surplus variable (s ≥ 0) Subtracted from a ≥ constraint: amount by which requirement is exceeded. Coefficient 0 in Z.

 Artificial variable (a ≥ 0) Added to ≥ and = constraints only to get an initial identity (starting basis); has no physical meaning and
 must be driven to zero (penalty −M in Max, +M in Min, or Phase I).

 Basic variable A variable in the current basis (column of the identity matrix); any variable which is non-negative when
 the other variables are put to zero. No. of basic variables = no. of constraints (rows).

 cj , CB cj = objective coefficient of variable j; CB = coefficients of the basic variables.

 zj zj = Σ (CB × entries of column j) — e.g. (CB×x1) + (CB×x1) + … ; z under RHS = current Z.

 cj − zj (net evaluation) Net gain in Z per unit of variable j brought in. For a Max problem a positive cj − zj means the current
 solution is not optimal. Basic variables always have cj − zj = 0.

 Key (pivot) column Column with the most positive cj − zj → its variable enters.

 Ratio θ (limiting ratio) RHS ÷ corresponding element of the key column, only for positive elements (ignore 0 and negative).

 Key row / key element Row with the smallest non-negative θ → its basic variable leaves. Intersection of key row and key
 column = key (pivot) element.


Simplex algorithm (Maximisation)

 1. Write the problem in standard form: make all bi ≥ 0; add slack to ≤, subtract surplus and add artificial to ≥, add artificial to =.
 (For Min Z, use Max Z* = −Z.)

 2. Form the initial simplex table with the slack/artificial variables as the starting basis (identity matrix). Initial solution: decision
 variables = 0, basic variables = RHS.

 3. Compute zj and cj − zj. If all cj − zj ≤ 0 → optimal; stop.

 4. Choose the key column (largest positive cj − zj); compute θ; choose key row (minimum θ); identify key element.

 5. Make the new table: divide the key row by the key element (new key row); make every other element of the key column zero
 by row operations Ri(new) = Ri − (its key-column element) × new key row. Replace the leaving variable by the entering
 variable in the basis (with its cj).

 6. Repeat from step 3.

 2.5 Big-M (penalty) method

 Used for LPPs with ≥ or = constraints, where slack variables cannot provide a starting identity basis.

 It introduces artificial variables to obtain an initial basic feasible solution.

 A large penalty value M is assigned to artificial variables in the objective: −M for Max (and for Max Z* = −Z of a Min problem);
 equivalently +M in a direct Min formulation.

 Simplex iterations continue until all artificial variables leave the basis; then the optimum is read from the final table.

 If the optimality condition is reached while an artificial variable is still positive in the basis → no feasible solution (infeasible).

Constraint type Add Objective coefficient (Max form)

≤ + slack s 0

≥ − surplus s + artificial a s: 0, a: −M

= + artificial a −M

 2.6 Two-Phase method

Avoids the large number M (useful on computers, where M causes rounding errors).

 1. Phase I: Set up the problem with slack, surplus and artificial variables. Replace the objective by Max Z′ = −(sum of artificial
 variables) (all other coefficients 0). Solve by simplex.
 • If Max Z′ < 0 (an artificial remains positive) → the original LPP is infeasible; stop.
 • If Max Z′ = 0 → a BFS of the original problem has been found; go to Phase II.

 2. Phase II: Drop the artificial columns, restore the original objective coefficients in the cj row and CB column, recompute cj − zj
 and continue simplex until optimal.

 2.7 Unrestricted (free) variables

If a variable xj is unrestricted in sign (may be +, − or 0), simplex cannot handle it directly because it requires all variables ≥ 0.
Replace it by the difference of two non-negative variables: xj = xj′ − xj″, xj′, xj″ ≥ 0, in the objective and in every constraint. In the
final answer xj = xj′ − xj″ (at most one of them is positive in a BFS). Similarly a variable with xj ≤ 0 is replaced by xj = −xj′.

 2.9 Sensitivity analysis (post-optimality analysis)

 Sensitivity analysis is a technique used to determine how different values of an input affect a particular output under a given
 set of assumptions. In LP it studies how the optimal solution changes when the coefficients cj, bi (and aij) change — without
 solving the problem again.


Why important in OR: it helps decision-makers understand the robustness of optimal solutions. Objectives: (i) assess the
stability of the optimal solution; (ii) identify critical parameters; (iii) support decision-making under uncertainty; (iv) provide
insights for resource allocation and planning.

Focus areas: (1) objective function coefficients cj; (2) right-hand-side values bi of constraints; (3) constraint coefficients aij (less
common).

Notes Q: What happens if we provide additional resources to the optimal solution?
 ① If the binding constraint (resource fully used) is relaxed: profit/cost improves right away; every extra unit adds value
 equal to its shadow price; works only up to the allowable increase limit.
 ② If it is a non-binding constraint (leftover/unused resource): nothing happens to the final answer or profit; you only end
 up with more unused slack (“junk”).
 Q: What if we change a coefficient of the objective function? Changing cj tilts the slope of the profit/cost line, but the
 feasible region stays unchanged. Within allowable limits the optimal product quantities (x1, x2) remain exactly the same,
 but the total profit/cost Z changes.
 Q: What is a dual price / shadow price? With every unit increment in RHS, the change in the value of the objective function
 (within the range for which the solution stays feasible).



 PYQ Final Exam 2025-26, Part B Q6(a): The sensitivity report shows a positive shadow price for a resource. How can the
 company use it to decide whether to increase that resource, and estimate the impact on profit?
 Model answer: ① A positive shadow price means the constraint is binding — the resource is fully used and is limiting
 profit. ② It is the increase in optimal profit per extra unit of that resource. ③ Decision rule: buy/add more of the
 resource only if its cost per unit is less than the shadow price (net gain = shadow price − cost per unit). ④ Impact
 estimate: Δ profit ≈ shadow price × Δ bi, valid only while Δ bi stays within the allowable increase of the RHS range; beyond
 it the basis changes and the model must be re-solved. ⑤ Example (Example 2.26): shadow price of resource 1 = 3, so 10
 more units add about Rs. 30, as long as the increase is within the allowable range. A resource with shadow price 0 has
 slack and should not be increased.

 2.10 Duality

 Every LPP (the primal) has an associated LPP called its dual, built from the same data. The optimal objective values of the
 two are equal, and the solution of one gives the solution of the other.


Why find the dual? (notes) • It may be easier to solve than the primal (e.g. many constraints, few variables). • It provides the
same optimal value as the primal (strong duality). • It gives the shadow prices (values of resources). • It is used to verify
optimality using complementary slackness. Relation to LPP solution: primal and dual have the same optimal objective value at
the optimum, so solving one helps determine the solution of the other.

Rules for writing the dual

 1. Put the primal in canonical form: for Max all constraints “≤”, for Min all constraints “≥” (multiply a wrong-way inequality by
 −1; an equality gives an unrestricted dual variable).

 2. The objective of the dual is opposite to that of the primal (Max ↔ Min).

 3. The RHS of the primal constraints become the coefficients of the dual objective; primal objective coefficients become the
 dual RHS.

 4. The coefficient matrix of the dual is the transpose AT of the primal matrix.

 5. Each primal constraint ↔ one dual variable wi; each primal variable ↔ one dual constraint.

Duality theorems / results

1. Dual of the dual is the primal.

2. Weak duality: for any feasible X of a Max primal and any feasible W of its dual, Z = CX ≤ bTW = W(dual). Any dual-feasible
 value is an upper bound on the primal.

3. Strong (fundamental) duality: if either problem has a finite optimum, so does the other and Max Z = Min W.

4. Unboundedness ↔ infeasibility: if the primal is unbounded, the dual is infeasible (and vice-versa). Both can also be
 infeasible.

5. Complementary slackness: at optimality, (primal slack of constraint i) × wi = 0 and (dual surplus of constraint j) × xj = 0. A
 resource with positive slack has shadow price 0; a positive variable makes its dual constraint tight.

6. Reading the dual from the primal optimal table: wi = zj of the slack (or −(cj − zj)) of constraint i; for a ≥ constraint use its
 surplus column (with sign change); for artificial-only rows use zj of the artificial minus its penalty.

 2.11 Dual simplex method

Used when the starting table is optimal but infeasible (all cj − zj ≤ 0 for Max, but some RHS < 0) — typical for Min problems with
≥ constraints (no artificials needed) and after adding a Gomory cut or a new constraint in sensitivity analysis.

 1. Convert to Max; multiply every ≥ constraint by −1 to make it ≤; add slacks (starting basis). Check that all cj − zj ≤ 0 (dual
 feasibility).

 2. If all RHS ≥ 0 → optimal and feasible; stop.

 3. Leaving variable: the basic variable with the most negative RHS (key row).

 4. Entering variable: among columns with a negative element arj in the key row, compute |(cj − zj) / arj| and pick the smallest
 (this keeps all cj − zj ≤ 0). If no arj < 0 → no feasible solution.

 5. Pivot exactly as in ordinary simplex; repeat.

 2.12 Primal–dual relationships and the primal–dual algorithm

Primal–dual computations: any simplex table carries both solutions — primal values in the RHS column, dual values in the zj row
under the starting-basis (slack) columns. The primal simplex keeps primal feasibility and works towards dual feasibility
(optimality); the dual simplex keeps dual feasibility and works towards primal feasibility. At the optimum both hold together and
Z = W.

Primal–dual algorithm (Dantzig–Ford–Fulkerson): start from any dual-feasible solution W; form a restricted primal using only the
primal variables whose dual constraints are tight (complementary slackness); solve it (minimising artificial infeasibility, as in
Phase I). If the restricted primal reaches zero infeasibility, the current pair is optimal; otherwise use its dual solution to improve
W while keeping dual feasibility, and repeat. It combines the ideas of Phase I and the dual simplex and is the basis of the
Hungarian method of Unit 4 (which is a primal–dual algorithm for the assignment problem).

Unit 3 — Integer Programming Problem (IPP)

 3.1 What is an IPP and why not just round off?

 An Integer Programming Problem is an LPP in which some or all decision variables are restricted to integer values. The LPP
 obtained by dropping the integer restriction is called its LP relaxation.


 Type Meaning

 Pure (all-integer) IPP All decision variables must be integers.

 Mixed IPP (MILP) Only some variables must be integers.

 Zero–one (binary) IPP Variables can be only 0 or 1 (yes/no decisions: select a project, open a plant, assign a job).



 Case from the notes. You are identifying the number of persons and machines for a job. You formulate an LPP, apply
 simplex and get: no. of persons = 6.25, no. of machines = 4.18. Comment & remedy: fractional persons/machines are
 meaningless. If we round-off / ceil / floor: ① there can be problems with constraints — the rounded solution may not
 satisfy the constraints; ② the rounded values may give an objective value which is not optimal. ∴ Alternative methods are
 required to get the integer solution — Gomory’s cutting-plane method and the Branch & Bound method.


Key facts: (i) the LP relaxation optimum is a bound on the IPP optimum (upper bound for Max, lower bound for Min) because the
IPP feasible set is a subset of the LP feasible set; (ii) if the LP optimum happens to be integer it is also the IPP optimum; (iii) IPP
feasible points are lattice points inside the LP region — the IPP feasible set is not convex, which is why corner-point/simplex logic
is not enough by itself.


 3.2 Gomory’s cutting-plane method (fractional cut, pure IPP)

 1. Step 1: Solve the LPP ignoring integrality (simplex). If all basic variables are integers → done.

 2. Step 2: Since all the variables are not integers, the current solution is not acceptable; we need an additional cut (constraint).

 3. Step 3 (choose source row): check the fractional part of every basic variable; the row with the largest fractional part is the
 source row (ties: choose any).

 4. Step 4 (form the cut): write the source row Σ ajxj = b. Split each coefficient and the RHS into integer + fractional part, with the
 fractional part always non-negative (e.g. −2/3 = −1 + 1/3; 7/3 = 2 + 1/3). The cut is

 Σ f j xj ≥ f 0 ⇔ −Σ fj xj + g = −f0, g ≥ 0 (Gomorian slack)


 5. Step 5: add the new row to the optimal table; its RHS is negative → apply the dual simplex method to restore feasibility.

 6. Step 6: repeat Steps 3–5 until all basic variables are integers.


 Justification of the cut (notes). Moving all integer parts to one side: (integer expression) = f0 − Σ fjxj. The left side is an
 integer, f0 < 1 and Σ fjxj ≥ 0, so f0 − Σ fjxj must be an integer ≤ 0. Hence the fractional part on the RHS will always be ≤ the
 sum of fractional parts on the LHS: Σ fjxj ≥ f0. Turning the equation into this inequality cuts away the current non-integer
 (fractional) solution without eliminating any valid integer solution.

 3.3 Branch & Bound method

1. Step 1: Obtain the initial solution by treating the problem as an LPP (LP relaxation) — graphically or by simplex. Its Z is the
 initial upper bound (Max). If integer → optimal.

2. Step 2 (Branch): choose the variable with the largest fractional part, xj = v. Create two sub-problems: (1) original + xj ≤ ⌊v⌋
 and (2) original + xj ≥ ⌊v⌋ + 1. (No integer lies between them, so no integer solution is lost.)

3. Step 3: solve each sub-problem as an LPP (new corner points).

4. Step 4 (Bound / fathom): a node is not branched further if (a) it is infeasible, (b) its solution is all-integer — record it as a
 candidate; the best candidate gives the lower bound (Max), or (c) its Z is not better than the best integer Z found so far.

5. Step 5: continue branching on the remaining nodes until all are fathomed; the best integer candidate is optimal. Draw the
 tree and add it to the solution.

Unit 4 — Transportation and Assignment Problems

 4.1 Transportation problem — formulation

 The transportation problem finds how many units xij to ship from each source i (supply ai) to each destination j (demand bj)
 so that total transportation cost is minimum (or total profit maximum). It is a special LPP.


Notation (notes): supply a1, a2, …, am at sources i; demand b1, …, bn at destinations j; xij = quantity of material transported from i
to j; cij = unit cost of transporting material from i to j.


 Minimise Z = Σi=1..m Σj=1..n cij xij (objective function)
 subject to Σj xij ≤ ai ∀ i (cannot ship more than supply)
 Σi xij ≥ bj ∀ j (meet every demand)
 xij ≥ 0


When the problem is balanced (Σ ai = Σ bj) all constraints become equalities. The model has m × n variables and m + n
constraints, of which only m + n − 1 are independent — so a basic feasible solution has (at most) m + n − 1 positive allocations.

 Term Meaning

 Balanced TP Σ supply = Σ demand.

 Unbalanced TP Σ supply ≠ Σ demand — add a dummy row/column with zero cost.

 Feasible solution Non-negative allocations satisfying all rim (supply and demand) conditions.

 Basic feasible solution Feasible solution with at most m + n − 1 positive allocations and no closed loop among them.

 Non-degenerate BFS Exactly m + n − 1 allocations in independent positions.

 Degenerate BFS Fewer than m + n − 1 allocations (notes: “m + n − 1 > allocations → degeneracy”).

 Closed loop A path of horizontal and vertical moves, turning only at occupied cells (except the start), returning
 to the starting empty cell.

 Opportunity cost Δij cij − (ui + vj) for an unoccupied cell: change in cost per unit allocated to that cell.


Methods of solving (two stages): ① Finding an initial feasible solution — (a) North-West Corner Rule (NWCR), (b) Minimum
(Least) Cost Method, (c) Vogel’s Approximation Method or Penalty Cost Method. ② Finding/checking the optimal solution — (a)
Modified Distribution Method (MODI / u-v method), (b) Stepping-stone method.


 4.2 Initial basic feasible solution: NWCR, LCM, VAM

North-West Corner Rule

 1. Start at the north-west (top-left) cell. Allocate x11 = min(a1, b1).

 2. If the supply of the row is exhausted move down; if the demand of the column is satisfied move right; if both, move
 diagonally (and note that the solution will be degenerate).

 3. Continue until the south-east cell. Ignores costs — quick but usually expensive.



Unit 4 · Transportation & Assignment Made by Jay Naik Page 78 of 124

Least (minimum) cost method — statements from the notes

1. The allocation is done corresponding to the least cij in the table (allocate the maximum possible there).

2. In case of a tie, choose the cell wherein we can do the maximum allocation.

3. If there is still a tie, pick up any cell arbitrarily.

4. Cross out the satisfied row/column and repeat with the remaining table.

Vogel’s Approximation Method (VAM / penalty cost method)

1. Penalty = difference between the two smallest cij values in each row and each column.

2. Select the row/column with the highest penalty; allocate as much as possible to the smallest cij cell in it.

3. Cross out the exhausted row/column, recompute penalties for the remaining table, and repeat. (Ties in penalty: choose the
 line with the least cost cell / where maximum allocation is possible.)

4. VAM takes you closest to the minimum cost — the best of the three starting methods.

 4.3 Modified Distribution (MODI / u-v) method

1. Start with a basic feasible solution (from NWCR/LCM/VAM). Verify that allocations = m + n − 1 (m = no. of rows, n = no. of
 columns). If fewer → degenerate: add ε (see 4.4).

2. For every allocated cell write ui + vj = cij. Put ui = 0 for the row with the most allocations and solve for all ui, vj.

3. For every unallocated cell compute the opportunity cost Δij = cij − (ui + vj).

4. If all Δij ≥ 0 → optimal (if some Δij = 0 → alternate optimal solution exists). Stop.

5. Otherwise choose the most negative Δij cell; draw a closed loop starting there with alternate +θ / −θ signs at the corners
 (corners at allocated cells).

6. θ = minimum allocation among the “−θ” cells. Add θ at “+” cells, subtract at “−” cells; the cell that becomes zero leaves.
 Repeat from step 2.

 4.5 Assignment problem — formulation

 The assignment problem assigns n jobs to n persons/machines/locations, one job to one person, so that total cost (or time)
 is minimum or total profit is maximum. By default assignment problems are minimisation problems.


Assignment is a special type of transportation problem in which every supply = 1 and every demand = 1.

 Minimise Z = Σi Σj cij xij (objective)
 xij = 1 if job i is assigned to person j, 0 otherwise
 Σj=1..n xij = 1 ∀ i (each job to exactly one person)
 Σi=1..n xij = 1 ∀ j (each person gets exactly one job)


Because only n of the 2n − 1 basic cells are positive, an assignment problem is a highly degenerate transportation problem —
that is why a special method (Hungarian) is used instead of MODI.

 Transportation problem Assignment problem

 Supplies ai and demands bj can be any quantities. Every supply and demand = 1; matrix must be square (balanced: rows = columns).

 xij ≥ 0 any quantity. xij ∈ {0, 1}.

 Solved by NWCR/LCM/VAM + MODI. Solved by the Hungarian method.

 BFS has m + n − 1 allocations. Exactly n assignments (degenerate as a TP).



 4.6 Hungarian method

 1. Balance: check no. of rows = no. of columns (balanced condition); otherwise add a dummy row/column of zeros.

 2. Step 1 – Row reduction: subtract the minimum value in each row from each element of that row.

 3. Step 2 – Column reduction: subtract the minimum value of each column from each element of that column.

 4. Step 3 – Assign: move row-wise and mark the first unique zero (a row with exactly one zero) with □ and cross (×) all other
 zeros in its column; then do the same column-wise. Repeat until no more marking is possible. If the number of □ = n →
 optimal.

 5. Step 4 – Minimum lines (ticking procedure): ① tick all unassigned rows; ② if there is a zero in a ticked row, tick its column;
 ③ if a ticked column has an assignment, tick its row; repeat ②–③ until no more ticking is possible. Draw lines through
 unticked rows and ticked columns (no. of lines = no. of assignments — checkpoint).

 6. Step 5 – Adjust: θ = minimum of the numbers through which no line is passing. Subtract θ from all uncovered elements, add
 θ where two lines intersect; elements with a single line passing do not change. Go back to Step 3.

Variation Treatment Example

Maximisation Put a negative sign before every cij and then subtract the smallest value from each row 4.17, 4.19,

 PYQ Unit 4 theory questions from past papers

 Re-Exam 2024-25 Q1(b): “Describe the three methods for an initial feasible solution of a TP. What is the purpose of
 MODI?” → NWCR (start top-left, allocate min(supply, demand), move right/down — quick but ignores cost), LCM
 (allocate to the cheapest cell first), VAM (penalty = difference of two lowest costs in each row/column; allocate in the
 least-cost cell of the line with the highest penalty — usually closest to optimal); see section 4.2. MODI tests a basic
 feasible solution for optimality using ui + vj = cij and Δij = cij − (ui + vj), and improves it with a closed loop until all Δij ≥ 0
 (section 4.3).

 Final 2024-25 Q1(b): “Explain how the Hungarian method is used, for balanced and unbalanced situations.” →
 Balanced (n × n): row reduction, column reduction, assign zeros, cover zeros with minimum lines, θ-adjust until n
 assignments (section 4.6, Examples 4.13, 4.14). Unbalanced: first add dummy rows/columns with 0 cost to make the
 matrix square; the person/job matched to the dummy stays idle; then proceed as balanced (Examples 4.17, 4.18).

 Final 2025-26 Q6(c): “Difference between maximisation and minimisation assignment problems; how does it change
 the approach? Show with a small example.” → The Hungarian method only minimises. For maximisation, first convert:
 subtract every entry from the largest entry (opportunity loss) or multiply every entry by −1; then solve as a
 minimisation and read the value from the original table. Small example (2 × 2 profits 5 8 / 7 6): loss matrix (8 − p) = 3 0
 / 1 2 → row reduce: 3 0 / 0 1 → assign A→2, B→1 → profit 8 + 7 = 15 (the other way gives only 11). Worked cases:
 Examples 4.19, 4.20, 4.17.

Term / rule One-line meaning

Operations Research Scientific, interdisciplinary, quantitative approach to decision-making for man–machine–money
 systems using limited resources.

Origin / milestones WWII England (military); 1948 OR Club UK; 1950 ORSA; 1953 ORI at ISI Calcutta; 1957 ORSI
 (Mahalanobis, 2nd 5-Year Plan) & IFORS.

Features of OR Decision-making tool, scientific approach, inter-disciplinary team, use of computers, system
 objectives.

Optimising performance measure E = f(Xc, Xuc): choose controllable variables to max/min the measure of effectiveness subject to
 constraints.

Deterministic vs stochastic Fixed known parameters (LP, TP, CPM, EOQ) vs random parameters (queues, PERT, simulation).

Models by function Normative (LP), predictive (exit polls), descriptive (plant layout).

Models by structure Iconic (blueprint), analogue (pressure gauge, contour map), symbolic (verbal, mathematical).

Models by time / method Static vs dynamic; analytical vs heuristic (not optimal) vs simulation.

Phases of OR Formulate → construct model → input data → solve → validate → implement → modify →
 establish controls.

LPP components Decision variables, linear objective, linear constraints, non-negativity.

Matrix form Max/Min Z = CX, AX (≤ = ≥) b, X ≥ 0.

LPP assumptions Proportionality, additivity, divisibility, certainty, linearity, non-negativity, finiteness.

Hyperplane / half-plane a·x = b / a·x ≤ b; with boundary = closed half-plane.

Convex set Segment joining any two points stays inside; LPP feasible region is convex.

Convex polyhedron Intersection of finitely many closed half-spaces.

Extreme point Corner not lying between two other points of the set; optimum occurs at one.

Basic / BFS / degenerate BFS Set n − m variables 0 and solve; BFS if all ≥ 0; degenerate if a basic variable = 0. Max no. = nCm.

Graphical steps Lines from intercepts → shade feasible side → corner points → evaluate Z (or iso-profit line).

Graphical: infeasible No common region (Ex 2.8).

Graphical: unbounded Open region and Z improves without limit (Ex 2.9).

Graphical: redundant Constraint not touching/changing the region (Ex 2.7).

Graphical: alternate optima Objective parallel to a binding edge; two corners tie (Ex 2.10).

Graphical: degenerate More than two lines through the optimal corner (Ex 2.11).

Slack / surplus / artificial +s for ≤; −s + a for ≥; +a for =. Artificial cost −M (Max form).

zj, cj − zj zj = Σ CB·aij; Max problem optimal when all cj − zj ≤ 0.

Entering / leaving (primal) Most positive cj − zj enters; minimum positive ratio θ = RHS / key-column element leaves.

Pivot operation New key row = old ÷ key element; other rows: R − (key-col element) × new key row.

Min problem Max Z* = −Z; Zmin = −Z*max.

Big-M Penalty M on artificials; artificial positive at optimum ⇒ infeasible.

Two-phase Phase I: Max Z′ = −Σa; Z′ < 0 ⇒ infeasible; Phase II with original objective (drop artificials).

Primal unbounded ⇒ dual infeasible.

Fractional part rule Always non-negative: −2/3 = −1 + 1/3.

Branch & Bound Branch x ≤ ⌊v⌋ / x ≥ ⌊v⌋+1 on largest fraction; fathom if infeasible, integer, or bound not better.

LCM Allocate to least cost cell; tie → max allocation; still tie → arbitrary.

VAM Penalty = difference of two smallest costs; highest penalty line, least cost cell; best start.

m + n − 1 rule Non-degenerate BFS has exactly m + n − 1 independent allocations.

MODI ui + vj = cij (occupied); Δij = cij − (ui + vj) (empty); all Δ ≥ 0 ⇒ optimal.

Closed loop & θ Loop from most negative Δ cell, ± signs alternate; θ = min at “−” cells.
